summary:
San Marino decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 1864. A residual provision, Article 274 of the Criminal Code, punished habitual homosexual acts causing public scandal with three months to one year of imprisonment; it was repealed in September 2004 and was never reported as applied. No criminal penalty attaches to gender identity, and no statute regulates which bathrooms or facilities a person may use.

Entry carries no documented friction. The border with Italy is open, and no identity screening that risks outing an arriving visitor is recorded.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. The 2026 edition of the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map lists San Marino among the countries with no functioning legal or administrative process for changing a gender marker. The consequence falls on residents rather than travellers: a visitor's foreign documents govern throughout a stay, and no domestic procedure exists that could alter them.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation is prohibited in primary law. A referendum held on 2 June 2019 carried with 71.46% in favour, inserting a prohibition on sexual-orientation discrimination into Article 4 of the Declaration of Citizens' Rights. The Penal Code has outlawed discrimination and hate speech on sexual-orientation grounds since 3 May 2008 and provides penalty enhancements for hate crimes so motivated. In November 2019 San Marino accepted Universal Periodic Review recommendations to outlaw discrimination based on gender identity, the only protection machinery in the sources that speaks to trans people directly.

There are occasionally reports of violence and hate crimes against the LGBTI community. No pattern of anti-trans violence is documented in this small, tourism-dependent country.

Civil unions have been in force since 5 December 2018 and fully operational since 11 February 2019, granting couples rights over residency and citizenship, pensions, healthcare, succession and stepchild adoption. Sammarinese same-sex couples remain barred from marriage. A December 2017 budget-law amendment permitted foreign same-sex couples to marry in San Marino to encourage tourism, but as of 2024 the implementing legislation does not appear to have been drafted, so a visitor should not expect to complete a marriage here.
tangentialFactors:
San Marino's relationship-recognition law, approved by the legislature in November 2018, was described at the time as leaner than the equivalent Italian statute, a comparison that reflects how closely Sammarinese social policy is read against its much larger neighbour.

Political symbolism runs ahead of the statutory text. Paolo Rondelli was appointed captain regent on 4 April 2022, the world's first openly gay head of state; the post is held for six months and carries no executive power. The same reporting notes that homosexuality was punishable by jail time in San Marino until 2004 and that legal recognition of gay couples followed in 2016.

Public visibility has been limited. Until recently LGBTQ people in San Marino went unnoticed, with very few public debates in media, society or politics, and in the early 2000s the government rejected LGBTQ groups' request to recognise 17 May as the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia. The 2019 referendum and the 2022 appointment mark the visible shift from that period.

The country's sex education programme, together with emotional education programmes, expressly provides for knowledge of LGBTQ rights, and the Curriculum of Education to Citizenship also covers LGBTQ matters. San Marino was one of 12 countries examined in the 34th session of the Universal Periodic Review Working Group in November 2019, and the SOGIESC recommendations it received and accepted are documented in ILGA's compilation.
localsOnly:
Civil unions confer residency and citizenship rights, pension entitlements, healthcare access, succession rights and stepchild adoption on the couples who register them. Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and no custody-specific provisions are recorded.

Discrimination and hate speech on sexual-orientation grounds have been offences in the Penal Code since 3 May 2008, with sentence enhancements where the crime is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. Sexual-orientation discrimination was added to Article 4 of the Declaration of Citizens' Rights by the referendum of 2 June 2019, which passed with 71.46% in favour after a March 2019 council vote of 35 for, 8 against and 1 abstention fell short of the 39 votes required.

Gay and bisexual men are permitted to donate blood. The age of consent is 14 for both opposite-sex and same-sex sexual acts, and it is an offence to incite a minor under 18 to sexual corruption.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Legal Gender Recognition chapter of the ILGA Annual Review 2026, which sets out country-by-country findings for 2025, does not carry a San Marino entry; the documented cases in that chapter concern Albania's rejection of a self-ID recommendation at UPR, trans activist Luana Myrto's legal action in Albania, and Andorra's delayed hormone-treatment decree. Whether any Sammarinese development occurred in 2025 is therefore unresolved on these sources.

The scope of the gender-identity discrimination prohibition accepted at UPR in November 2019, and whether it has since been enacted in statute, is not sourced here.

No source in this inventory reports trans-specific violence, its perpetrators, or outcomes of prosecutions; the references to occasional violence and hate crimes concern the LGBTI community generally and are undated.

Whether the December 2017 amendment permitting foreign same-sex couples to marry has acquired implementing legislation after 2024 is unresolved. The absence of any statute on bathroom or facility access is stated as an absence of regulation, not as a judicial or administrative ruling on the point.
